title: Guyana’s Oil Boom Matters More Than Ever | OilPrice.com
text:
Glencore Sees $3.3 Billion Trading Profit as Iran War Rattles Oil Markets

As Oilprice’s South America correspondent, I cover Colombia (where I currently live), Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Guyana, Suriname and Uruguay. I…

In a surprise development, the tiny South American nation of Guyana recently emerged as a major oil exporter. In a mere four years, the former British colony of one million went from first discovery to first oil. Guyana has cemented its place among South America’s leading oil producers, pumping nearly one million barrels per day, making it the continent’s third-largest oil producer. The rapid expansion of Guyana’s offshore oil industry will enhance energy security in the Americas at a crucial time, with heightened Middle East tensions sharply impacting global supply.

Official government data shows Guyana lifted 888,000 barrels of crude oil per day at the end of May 2026. This was 4% lower than the 924,000 barrels being extracted at the start of the month. There are four active floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) vessels operating in offshore Guyana, with a fifth, named the Errea Wittu, expected to start up during 2026 when the Uaru project comes online. ExxonMobil’s $12.7 billion Uaru project, upon reaching capacity, will add 250,000 barrels per day to Guyana’s petroleum output, lifting production over one million barrels daily.

This will allow the former British colony to surpass Venezuela, making it South America’s second-largest oil producer behind Brazil. While Caracas has expanded production since January 2026, growth is constrained by the need to rebuild Venezuela’s heavily corroded petroleum infrastructure, which will require tens of billions of dollars and at least a decade. Speaking of Venezuela, Washington’s decision to intervene in the near-failed state at the start of 2026 removed the most serious threat to Guyana’s burgeoning petroleum boom.

You see, President Nicolas Maduro, for years, threatened to annex the mineral-rich Essequibo, a western region the size of the state of Georgia. This territorial dispute dates to the nineteenth century when Guyana was a British colony. The Essequibo comprises around two-thirds of Guyana’s territory. By 2024, Caracas was repeatedly threatening to invade the territory. The disputed region’s territorial waters contain the Exxon-operated 6.6-million-acre Stabroek Block, which holds an estimated 11 billion barrels of oil and Guyana’s only operational oilfields.

Aside from Uaru, Exxon is developing three additional projects in the Stabroek Block. The first slated for completion is the $12.5 billion Whiptail facility, which is Exxon’s sixth project in Guyana. The project is expected to come online in late 2027 with oil lifted from 48 production and injection wells by the Jaguar FPSO. The facility will have a capacity of 250,000 barrels per day. Whiptail will be followed by the $6.8 billion Hammerhead project with a capacity of 150,000 barrels per day from 18 production and injection wells. Hammerhead is slated to commence operation during 2029.

Exxon’s eighth project in offshore Guyana is the Longtail development. It is anticipated that a final investment decision (FID) for the $12.5 billion project will be made in late 2026 or early 2027. Longtail will have a nameplate capacity of 1.2 billion cubic feet of natural gas and 250,000 barrels of condensate per day, with the operation commencing operations in 2030. This facility marks a strategic decision by Exxon to start lifting natural gas in offshore Guyana. This decision couldn’t come at a better time, with many countries in South America, like Colombia, suffering from natural gas shortages, forcing them to import greater quantities of the fossil fuel.

Those facilities indicate just how rapidly Guyana’s oil production will expand. Indeed, it is anticipated the tiny South American country will be pumping up to 1.9 million barrels of crude oil, including condensate, by 2030. This will cement Guyana’s place as South America’s second largest oil producer behind Brazil, unless Venezuela proves capable of significantly boosting petroleum output over the same period, which is doubtful. That substantial increase in hydrocarbon output will go a long way to securing energy supply in the Americas.

Disruption to shipping passing through the Strait of Hormuz poses considerable risks to regional countries, like Colombia and Peru, which are increasingly dependent on fuel and other hydrocarbon imports. Heightened Middle East tensions, along with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, see greater demand from countries in Asia and Europe for oil that is not shipped through the vital choke point. As a result, demand for Guyana’s petroleum is soaring ever higher, just as it is for neighboring Brazil, with China now receiving most of that country’s petroleum exports.

The largest buyers of Guyana’s crude oil are the United States, the Netherlands, Italy, and Panama. Indeed, the volume of Guyana’s oil shipments to the U.S. has been climbing at a solid clip since 2020.

According to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), the world’s largest economy received an average of 261,000 barrels per day during April 2026. This number is 51% greater than for the same month two years earlier and nearly seven times greater than the 38,000 barrels per day imported from Guyana in April 2022. While this is only a thirtieth of the 7.9 million barrels per day imported for that period, the volume of crude oil shipments received from Guyana is expected to grow as production expands.

Guyana’s massive oil boom, which is still in the early stages of development, is rewriting the global energy map. Along with Brazil and Argentina, the former British colony is leading a major surge in non-OPEC petroleum production growth.
